query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, trace addition of boron during alloy processing will promote its segregation at the internal lamellar boundaries, thereby enhancing interfacial cohesion and suppressing microcrack initiation. This targeted segregation is predicted to improve both the room-temperature tensile strength and ductility of the eutectic high-entropy alloy relative to the unmodified baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor addition of boron during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Boron content must be optimized to be low enough to avoid the formation of brittle boride phases, and processing parameters (such as cooling rate and annealing conditions) should be tuned to ensure effective boron segregation at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The boron segregates to the internal boundaries, enhancing atomic bonding and transitioning the failure mode from brittle interfacial decohesion to more uniform, cohesive deformation, thereby mitigating microcrack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Both tensile strength and ductility at room temperature will improve compared to the baseline alloy, as microcrack nucleation at the lamellar boundaries is suppressed.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar microstructure that suffers from a strength-ductility trade-off due to brittle interfacial failure.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected under room-temperature tensile deformation conditions provided that the boron level is carefully controlled to prevent the emergence of brittle boride phases and that the processing conditions facilitate its proper segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum boron concentration and precise processing conditions for achieving enhanced segregation without forming detrimental phases require further empirical calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with varied trace boron concentrations, including a control with no boron. Use identical processing conditions with controlled cooling rates and annealing protocols to encourage boron segregation. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to confirm the presence and distribution of boron at the lamellar boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to evaluate changes in strength and ductility, and conduct fractographic analysis to assess the failure mode.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strength and ductility (elongation at fracture)
Microstructural analysis via TEM and APT (for boron segregation and identification of any brittle boride phases)
Fractography to evaluate changes in crack initiation and propagation mechanisms
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if an increase in boron content does not result in a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if the microstructural analysis reveals the formation of brittle boride phases that negate or worsen mechanical properties.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies featuring numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking initiates during room-temperature tensile deformation.
frame.goal: To achieve a simultaneous improvement in tensile strength and ductility at room temperature by mitigating microcrack nucleation along internal boundaries.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing methods have been unable to eliminate room-temperature brittleness and limited ductility because they typically improve strength at the expense of ductility.
root_cause_cues: catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation
conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility
previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness
constraints: The intervention must be a single processing or compositional modification
It must improve both strength and ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline
The solution must operate under room-temperature tensile deformation conditions
prior_attempts: Numerous microstructural-design approaches and processing strategies (including conventional thermomechanical treatments) that enhance strength but reduce ductility
Attempts that modify colony features without addressing interfacial cracking
frame.understanding: The mechanism by which modifying interlamellar boundaries (e.g., by promoting solute segregation) can suppress microcrack initiation and propagate more uniform deformation across both phases.
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled minor addition of a segregating element such as boron during alloy processing will lead to its preferential segregation at the internal lamellar boundaries. This interfacial modification is expected to enhance atomic bonding and promote cohesive failure mechanisms over brittle interfacial decohesion. In turn, microcrack initiation will be suppressed, and both strength and ductility during room-temperature tensile deformation will improve relative to the unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy. The hypothesis holds provided that the boron content is optimized (i.e., not so high as to form brittle boride phases) and that processing parameters (like cooling rate) are tuned to enable the desired segregation. Prior evidence in steels and some high-entropy alloy systems demonstrates that trace boron additions can improve grain-boundary cohesion. An experiment to test this hypothesis would involve preparing a series of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with increasing boron content, characterizing microstructural changes at the boundaries (using transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography), and subjecting the samples to room-temperature tensile testing. A falsifying result would be if boron addition either leads to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at boundaries (revealed by microscopy) or if tensile tests fail to show any improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline alloy.
